title: A spectacle of cosmic dust from Paranal
caption: The zodiacal light, Venus and Mars beside the Antu telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A faint, bluish band of light climbs from the horizon beside one of the Very Large Telescope’s Unit Telescopes at ESO’s Paranal Observatory. This is the zodiacal light, sometimes called “false dawn” when it appears before sunrise.

It lines up with the ecliptic, the plane in which Earth orbits the Sun. That plane is full of tiny grains of dust that scatter sunlight, and the scattered light makes the glow. The other planets orbit in nearly the same plane, so they often show up inside it: Venus is the brightest point here, and Mars is a faint reddish dot up and to its right.

Many people have never seen the zodiacal light, because light pollution or even moonlight can wash it out. Fittingly, the telescope basking in this display of sunlight is named Antu, which means “the Sun” in Mapudungun, a language spoken in central-southern Chile.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to D. Gasparri/ESO. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: The zodiacal light is real and visible from very dark sites, but faint; a long exposure makes it much more obvious than it looks to the eye.

explore: The Atacama Desert still has skies dark enough for sights like this, a heritage ESO describes as worth protecting.
alt: A faint cone of bluish light rising from the horizon into a starry sky beside a large telescope building, with a bright point of light, Venus, inside the glow.
